aeo.what_is: Recurrent episodes of out-of-control eating without compensatory behaviors, causing significant distress and medical risk.

content.description: Binge Eating Disorder (BED) is characterized by recurrent episodes of eating an objectively large amount of food in a discrete period, accompanied by a sense of loss of control, and associated with marked distress. Unlike bulimia nervosa, BED does not involve regular inappropriate compensatory behaviors (e.g., purging, excessive exercise).
content.temporal_criteria: Binge eating episodes must occur, on average, at least once weekly for 3 months. Frequency determines severity: mild (1–3 episodes per week), moderate (4–7), severe (8–13), extreme (14+). Full remission requires absence of binge eating for a sustained period.
content.misdiagnosis_explained: Binge eating disorder is often missed because it's dismissed as 'overeating' or lack of self-control, especially in individuals with higher body weight where binge eating may be assumed rather than assessed. Medical providers may focus on weight management without exploring eating patterns or the sense of loss of control. BED can be confused with bulimia nervosa (which requires regular compensatory behaviors), night eating syndrome, or depression with increased appetite. The key distinction is recurrent, objectively large eating episodes with loss of control and marked distress, without regular purging, fasting, or excessive exercise to compensate.
content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Recurrent episodes of binge eating, defined as: 1) eating, in a discrete period (e.g., within any 2-hour period), an amount of food that is definitely larger than most people would eat under similar circumstances; and 2) a sense of lack of control over eating during the episode. B. Episodes are associated with ≥3 of: eating more rapidly than normal; eating until uncomfortably full; eating large amounts when not physically hungry; eating alone due to embarrassment; feeling disgusted, depressed, or very guilty afterward. C. Marked distress regarding binge eating. D. Occurs, on average, at least once a week for 3 months. E. Not associated with regular use of inappropriate compensatory behaviors and does not occur exclusively during anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa.
content.prevalence: Estimated lifetime prevalence ~2–3% in the general population; more common in females, but also prevalent in males. Frequently comorbid with obesity, metabolic syndrome, and mood disorders.
content.age_of_onset: Typically late adolescence to early adulthood; can emerge in childhood or later adulthood.
content.prognosis: Good recovery rates with evidence-based psychotherapy; relapse possible, especially under stress. Chronic untreated BED can lead to medical complications and worsened mental health outcomes.

circuitry: Hyperactivation of mesolimbic reward pathways (ventral striatum, nucleus accumbens) to food cues.
Reduced prefrontal inhibitory control during high-calorie food exposure.
Altered hypothalamic–gut–brain signaling (ghrelin, leptin, insulin resistance).
neurotransmitters: Serotonin involvement in satiety and mood regulation.
Endogenous opioid system activation during binge episodes.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Family history of mood disorders, obesity, or substance use increases risk; adverse childhood experiences and chronic dieting contribute.

history_psychosocial: Binge episode frequency, triggers, and loss-of-control experiences.
Body image concerns, emotional eating patterns, and comorbid mental health symptoms.
medical_assessment: Weight, BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure.
Screen for metabolic syndrome: fasting glucose, lipid panel, HbA1c.
Assess for sleep apnea, GERD, musculoskeletal pain.
standardized_measures: Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7)
risk_stratification: Identify severe depression, suicidality, or comorbid substance use.
Assess medical risk from obesity-related conditions.
differential_diagnosis: Bulimia Nervosa (presence of regular compensatory behaviors)
Depression with hyperphagia (without discrete binge episodes)
evaluation.team_and_process: Collaborative approach with therapist, dietitian, and medical provider; include psychiatry when considering pharmacotherapy.

behavioral: Eating large amounts of food quickly, even when not hungry.
Eating alone due to shame or embarrassment.
Frequent dieting without sustained weight loss.
emotional: Loss of control during eating episodes.
Feelings of guilt, shame, or depression afterward.
physical: Fluctuating weight or progressive weight gain.

biological: Genetic predisposition to obesity or mood disorders
Neurotransmitter dysregulation in dopamine and serotonin systems
environmental: Easy access to highly palatable, calorie-dense foods

impact_on_life.home: Conflict over eating behaviors, secrecy around food.
impact_on_life.school_work: Reduced productivity and concentration due to emotional distress.
impact_on_life.social: Avoidance of social eating situations; isolation.

psychotherapy: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) — gold standard, addresses binge triggers, cognitive distortions, and regular eating patterns.
Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) — focuses on interpersonal triggers and emotional regulation.
Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) — for emotion regulation and distress tolerance.
nutrition_rehabilitation: Structured meal planning to prevent extreme hunger and reduce binge risk.
Dietitian support to normalize eating patterns.
medical_management: Monitor metabolic health, treat comorbid medical conditions.
medications: SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline) for mood/anxiety and reduction in binge frequency.
Topiramate (off-label, may reduce binge frequency and aid weight loss).
lifestyle_interventions: Regular physical activity for health (not as a compensatory behavior).
Sleep hygiene to reduce stress eating.

treatment_goals: Eliminate binge episodes and restore control over eating.
Reduce medical risks associated with BED.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Assuming binge eating is simply 'overeating' without loss of control.
Focus on obesity without assessing for BED behaviors.
overdiagnosis_factors: Misinterpreting emotional eating as meeting full criteria.
Applying diagnosis to night eating syndrome or bulimia nervosa.
warning_signs: Hiding food or eating in secret.
self_help_strategies: Keep a food and mood journal to identify triggers.
Establish regular meal and snack times.
Engage in non-food coping activities for stress.

childhood: Episodes may involve sneaking or hiding food.
Often associated with early weight gain.
adolescence: Increased frequency with stress from school or peer relationships.
Risk of co-occurring depression or anxiety.
adulthood: Episodes tied to work stress, relationships, or life transitions.

first_person_statements: I'd eat until I felt physically sick, but I couldn't stop. The guilt afterward was crushing, and I'd promise myself 'never again,' but it kept happening.
Binge eating was my way of coping with stress and sadness. Food felt like comfort in the moment, but then I'd feel disgusted with myself.
I thought I just had no willpower, but learning it's a disorder helped me understand it's not about weakness—it's about my brain and emotions.
I hid my binge eating from everyone. I felt so ashamed that I was eating 'normally' in front of people but secretly bingeing alone.
Recovery taught me that restricting during the day was making the binges worse. Eating regular meals actually helped me stop bingeing.
Therapy helped me understand my triggers and develop healthier ways to cope with emotions instead of turning to food.

real_life_examples: A 19-year-old college student struggles with binge eating after starting school. She restricts calories during the day to 'save' for a binge, then eats large amounts of fast food, cookies, and chips late at night in her dorm room. She feels intense shame and guilt, affecting her mood and academic performance. Her roommate notices food wrappers and encourages her to seek help. She begins CBT with a therapist who helps her establish regular eating patterns, identify emotional triggers, and develop healthier coping skills. A dietitian guides her toward balanced meals without restriction. After 4 months, her binge episodes decrease from daily to rare, and she reports improved self-esteem and functioning.

A 35-year-old office worker has been binge eating for 5 years, often triggered by work stress and marital conflict. He eats thousands of calories in a single sitting—entire pizzas, ice cream, and snacks—feeling unable to stop. His weight has increased significantly, and he's been diagnosed with prediabetes and hypertension. After a health scare, he discloses his eating patterns to his doctor, who refers him to an eating disorder specialist. He starts lisdexamfetamine, which reduces binge urges, and participates in CBT focusing on emotional regulation and structured eating. He also attends couples therapy to address relationship stress. Over 6 months, his binge eating resolves, he loses weight gradually, and his metabolic markers improve.

A 16-year-old high schooler with a history of anxiety binges on food after arguments with her parents or when feeling overwhelmed by schoolwork. She eats large amounts rapidly, often in secret, then feels intense guilt and depression. She avoids social events and skips lunch at school out of shame. Her school counselor notices her distress and connects her with a therapist trained in DBT. She learns emotion regulation and distress tolerance skills, reducing her reliance on food to cope. Her parents participate in family sessions to improve communication and reduce conflict. After 8 weeks of treatment, her binge frequency decreases significantly, and she begins eating lunch with friends again.

A 42-year-old woman with chronic depression and a history of yo-yo dieting develops binge eating disorder. She binges multiple times per week, often late at night, eating large quantities of sweets, bread, and comfort foods. She feels hopeless about her weight and her ability to stop bingeing. Her therapist introduces Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT), which helps her address grief, role transitions, and interpersonal conflicts driving her binges. Her psychiatrist starts sertraline for depression, which also reduces binge frequency. With a dietitian's support, she establishes regular meals and stops restrictive dieting. After 9 months, she achieves full remission from binge eating and reports improved mood and relationships.

A 28-year-old man with BED binges almost daily, often consuming entire boxes of cereal, multiple burgers, and gallons of ice cream. He feels disgusted and ashamed but continues the cycle. His weight and blood pressure are climbing, and he feels socially isolated. He enters a partial hospitalization program where he receives intensive CBT, group therapy, meal support, and medical monitoring. He learns to recognize hunger and fullness cues, challenge all-or-nothing thinking, and use mindfulness to manage urges. After 6 weeks of PHP and transition to outpatient care, his binge eating stops, and he maintains recovery with weekly therapy and regular dietitian visits.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve recurrent episodes of binge eating with a sense of loss of control, often triggered by restriction or negative emotions.
comparisons.differences: In bulimia nervosa, binges are regularly followed by compensatory behaviors (purging, fasting, excessive exercise) to prevent weight gain. In binge eating disorder, there are no regular compensatory behaviors. BED is also more common in individuals with higher body weight, whereas bulimia is typically at normal or slightly above-normal weight.

comparisons.similarities: Both can involve episodes of binge eating and distress about eating and body image.
comparisons.differences: Anorexia nervosa requires significantly low body weight and is characterized by restriction with or without binge/purge episodes. Binge eating disorder occurs at normal or higher weight, and restriction is not the primary behavior—binge eating without compensation is.

comparisons.condition: Major Depressive Disorder with increased appetite
comparisons.similarities: Both can involve increased eating and emotional distress, with food used as a coping mechanism.
comparisons.differences: In depression, eating may increase due to low mood or neurovegetative symptoms, but without discrete, out-of-control binges. Binge eating disorder is defined by recurrent, objectively large eating episodes with loss of control and marked distress specifically about the eating behavior.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve recurrent episodes of eating that may be distressing and contribute to weight gain.
comparisons.differences: Night eating syndrome involves consuming a large portion of daily calories after dinner or during nighttime awakenings, but without the sense of loss of control that defines a binge. BED centers on discrete binge episodes, not specifically tied to nighttime, with marked distress and rapid consumption.

faqs.question: Is binge eating disorder just overeating or lack of willpower?
faqs.answer: No. Binge eating disorder is a serious mental health condition with biological, psychological, and environmental factors. It's characterized by recurrent, out-of-control eating episodes and significant distress—not simply eating too much occasionally or lacking discipline. It requires professional treatment.

faqs.question: How is binge eating disorder different from bulimia?
faqs.answer: The key difference is compensatory behaviors. Bulimia involves regular purging (vomiting, laxatives), fasting, or excessive exercise after binges to prevent weight gain. Binge eating disorder involves recurrent binges without these regular compensatory behaviors, leading to different medical and psychological profiles.

faqs.question: Do I have to be overweight to have binge eating disorder?
faqs.answer: No. While BED is more common in people with higher body weight, individuals at any weight can have binge eating disorder. The diagnosis is based on the pattern and distress of binge eating, not body size. Normal-weight individuals with BED still need and benefit from treatment.

faqs.question: Can binge eating disorder be treated without focusing on weight loss?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that's often the most effective approach. Treatment focuses on stopping binge eating, normalizing eating patterns, and addressing emotional triggers—not on dieting or weight loss, which can worsen binge eating. Many people find that their weight stabilizes or decreases naturally as binge eating resolves.

faqs.question: What causes binge eating disorder?
faqs.answer: BED arises from a combination of genetic predisposition, brain chemistry differences (especially in reward and impulse control), psychological factors (low self-esteem, perfectionism, emotion dysregulation), and environmental influences (dieting culture, stress, trauma, easy access to highly palatable foods). It's not caused by one single factor.

faqs.question: Is lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) the only medication for BED?
faqs.answer: Lisdexamfetamine is the only FDA-approved medication specifically for binge eating disorder. However, other medications like SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline) and topiramate (off-label) can also reduce binge frequency. Medication is most effective when combined with psychotherapy like CBT.

faqs.question: Can therapy really help stop binge eating?
faqs.answer: Yes. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is the gold-standard treatment for BED and has strong evidence for reducing and eliminating binge episodes. CBT helps you identify triggers, challenge distorted thoughts, normalize eating patterns, and develop healthier coping strategies. Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) and Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) are also effective.

faqs.question: Why do I binge even when I'm not hungry?
faqs.answer: Binge eating is often triggered by emotions (stress, sadness, boredom, loneliness), dietary restriction (which increases both physical and psychological urges to eat), or learned habits. It's not about physical hunger—it's about coping, reward-seeking, or breaking free from restriction. Treatment addresses these underlying drivers.

faqs.question: How long does recovery from binge eating disorder take?
faqs.answer: It varies. Some people see significant improvement within a few months of starting CBT or medication, while others need longer or more intensive treatment. Early engagement, reducing restrictive eating, addressing emotional triggers, and building support systems all improve the speed and likelihood of recovery.

faqs.question: Will I gain weight if I start eating regularly to stop binge eating?
faqs.answer: Most people maintain or even lose weight when they stop binge eating and establish regular, balanced meals. Binge episodes often involve consuming thousands of calories, and eliminating them—even while eating more regularly—typically results in lower overall intake and weight stabilization or loss over time.

faqs.question: Can stress cause binge eating disorder?
faqs.answer: Stress is a common trigger for binge eating episodes, but it doesn't directly cause the disorder. BED develops from a combination of genetic vulnerability, brain differences, and environmental factors like chronic dieting, trauma, or weight stigma. Learning healthier stress management is a key part of treatment.

faqs.question: Can binge eating disorder lead to other health problems?
faqs.answer: Yes. BED is associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, heart disease, sleep apnea, and joint problems. It also increases risk for depression, anxiety, and social isolation. Early treatment reduces these risks and improves overall health and quality of life.

faqs.question: Is it normal to feel ashamed about binge eating?
faqs.answer: Shame is very common with BED, but it's not your fault. The disorder creates a cycle of secrecy and guilt that makes it harder to seek help. Opening up to a healthcare provider or therapist is an important first step. Treatment helps reduce shame and build self-compassion alongside stopping binge eating.

faqs.question: Can I recover from BED on my own?
faqs.answer: While some people reduce symptoms independently, professional treatment significantly improves outcomes and speeds recovery. Self-help resources (books, apps) can be useful supplements, but evidence-based therapy, medical monitoring, and nutritional counseling are key to addressing the root causes and preventing relapse.

faqs.question: Why does dieting make my binge eating worse?
faqs.answer: Restriction—whether physical (cutting calories) or psychological (labeling foods 'bad')—increases hunger, preoccupation with food, and the likelihood of binge eating. Dieting creates a deprivation-binge cycle. Treatment focuses on regular, balanced eating without restriction, which paradoxically reduces binge urges and frequency.

faqs.question: Can men have binge eating disorder?
faqs.answer: Yes. BED affects people of all genders and is more evenly distributed between men and women than other eating disorders. Men may be underdiagnosed due to stigma and misconceptions that eating disorders only affect women. Symptoms, risks, and treatments are similar across genders.

faqs.question: What should I do if I binge eat?
faqs.answer: After a binge, practice self-compassion—shame and punishment fuel the cycle. Return to your regular eating pattern as soon as possible (don't skip the next meal). Use coping skills like journaling, calling a support person, or going for a walk. If binge eating is recurrent, seek professional help from a therapist or eating disorder specialist.

faqs.question: Is binge eating disorder genetic?
faqs.answer: There is a genetic component—heritability is estimated around 40–60%. Having a family history of eating disorders, obesity, mood disorders, or substance use increases risk. However, genes interact with environmental and psychological factors, so it's not predetermined. Treatment is effective regardless of genetic risk.

faqs.question: Can children and teens have binge eating disorder?
faqs.answer: Yes. BED can develop in childhood or adolescence, often triggered by dieting, peer pressure, family stress, or bullying. Early intervention is crucial to prevent long-term health and psychological consequences. Treatment for youth often involves family-based approaches alongside individual therapy.

faqs.question: What is the difference between binge eating and emotional eating?
faqs.answer: Emotional eating involves eating in response to emotions (comfort eating), but without necessarily consuming objectively large amounts or experiencing loss of control. Binge eating disorder is defined by recurrent, large-volume eating episodes with loss of control and marked distress. Not all emotional eating is binge eating.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek help if you experience recurrent loss of control over eating, significant distress, or health problems related to eating behaviors.

positive_factors: Willingness to engage in structured eating patterns
challenging_factors: Significant weight stigma or repeated dieting failures

tiles.title: What is Binge Eating Disorder?
tiles.summary: Recurrent episodes of out-of-control eating without compensatory behaviors like purging or fasting.

tiles.title: Signs & Symptoms
tiles.summary: Eating large amounts rapidly, loss of control, eating when not hungry, shame, and marked distress.

tiles.title: Causes & Risk Factors
tiles.summary: Genetic predisposition, brain reward differences, chronic dieting, emotional dysregulation, and stress.

tiles.title: How It's Diagnosed
tiles.summary: Clinical interview about binge patterns, loss of control, distress, and absence of compensatory behaviors.

tiles.title: Treatment Options
tiles.summary: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), lisdexamfetamine, SSRIs, nutritional counseling, and IPT or DBT.

tiles.title: Medical Complications
tiles.summary: Obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, and depression or anxiety.

tiles.title: Recovery & Prognosis
tiles.summary: Good recovery rates with therapy. Regular eating and addressing triggers lead to lasting improvement.

tiles.title: Living with BED
tiles.summary: Structured meals, reducing restriction, managing emotional triggers, and maintaining therapy support.

tiles.title: Getting Help
tiles.summary: Seek professional care for recurrent binge eating, loss of control, or significant distress.
